name: Chromosomes
kicker: Coiled DNA-and-protein bundles that carry genes · 23 pairs per human cell
briefing: Chromosomes are tightly coiled bundles of DNA and protein that carry an organism’s genes, becoming visible under a microscope only when a cell is dividing. Humans have 46 of them, arranged in 23 pairs, with one chromosome in each pair inherited from each parent. An extra or missing chromosome can cause conditions such as Down syndrome, from an extra copy of chromosome 21, or Turner syndrome, from a missing sex chromosome.
answerHtml: Chromosomes (accept X, Y, or sex chromosome; prompt on autosome; do not accept “chromatin”)

qb.tip: Several matches are for the more specific “X chromosome” line (Barr body, lyonization, fragile X) — see the Buzzer Trap; a “Down’s syndrome” tossup and an unrelated math “Z” tossup were excluded as off-topic. tossups.p: Expanding CGG repeats on the FMR1 gene can make one of these unusually “fragile,” prone to breaking under the microscope. Condensin and cohesin, two SMC-family proteins, bundle and organize them, while a protein complex called the kinetochore clamps onto a pinched region, the centromere, to grab hold of spindle fibers.
tossups.r: Mitosis then hands out an identical set of these to each of the two new daughter cells. Humans carry 46 of them, bundled in 23 matching pairs. For 10 points, name these thread-like structures, made of DNA coiled around histone proteins, that carry an organism’s genes.

tossups.p: In female cells, one copy in a matched pair is silenced through a process called lyonization, bundling into a dense clump known as a Barr body. During meiosis, a scaffold called the synaptonemal complex zips paired partners together, and their crossovers show up as X-shaped points called chiasmata.
tossups.r: An extra copy of number 21 causes Down syndrome, while a missing sex-determining copy in females causes Turner syndrome. For 10 points, name these DNA-and-protein structures, 23 pairs of which are found in every human cell.

tossups.p: A translocated, swapped piece nicknamed the “Philadelphia” version of one of these is linked to a type of leukemia. Giant “polytene” copies form in the salivary glands of fruit fly larvae, while in bacteria, these structures form simple circular loops instead of the linear ones found in human cells.
tossups.r: Pictures called karyotypes line them up by size so doctors can spot an extra or missing one, as in the trisomy that causes Down syndrome. For 10 points, name these structures that carry an organism’s genes, 46 of which are found in human cells.

tossups.p: Treating plant cells with the chemical colchicine can double how many of these a cell has, a trick plant breeders use with crops like wheat and seedless watermelon. A fern called the adder’s-tongue holds the record for the most of these in any plant, numbering over 1,200.
tossups.r: A spore-making “sporophyte” stage in ferns and mosses carries twice as many of these as its “gametophyte” stage. Humans instead carry just 46, in 23 matched pairs. For 10 points, name these thread-like carriers of genetic information.

tossups.p: A pinched region on each of these, called the centromere, anchors a protein complex called the kinetochore to the cell’s spindle fibers during division. Condensin and cohesin, two SMC-family proteins, help organize and hold copies of these together before they split evenly between daughter cells.
tossups.r: Males born with an extra sex-determining one of these develop Klinefelter syndrome, while females missing one develop Turner syndrome. For 10 points, name these coiled bundles of DNA and protein, of which humans have 23 pairs.

tossups.p: Expanding repeats of the letters CGG on the FMR1 gene can make one of these unusually fragile. In fruit flies, oversized “polytene” copies of these form in the larval salivary glands, while a circular, non-linear form of these is typical in bacteria.

trap.title: Chromosomes, or just the X?
trap.body: This general answer line accepts specific sex-chromosome guesses like “X chromosome” or “Y chromosome,” since they are just examples. But several real tossups are built entirely around clues that only make sense for one specific chromosome — the X, including Barr bodies, lyonization, fragile X syndrome, or counting a single X (Turner syndrome) versus an extra one (Klinefelter syndrome).
trap.fix: If every clue in the question only makes sense for the X (or another single named one, like 21), give that specific name. If the clues mix in facts true of all of them — a count, karyotypes, mitosis, genes in general — the general answer is safe, and “chromatin” is never correct either way.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chromosomes (accept X/Y/sex/autosomal chromosome; prompt on autosome; do not accept or prompt on chromatin) — a related real tossup instead wants “X chromosome” specifically, and only prompts on bare “chromosome.”
